To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the participants in the study were able to draw upon different narratives to represent their identities, and their trajectories; (2) the participants were also able to draw upon these different discourses, and to respond to different regimes of language, as they negotiated their positions in different diasporas; (3) these narratives were not static, and were constantly being re-negotiated, in the context of changing political and ideological conditions; and (4) these narratives were also shaped by different

(1) narratives about ‘homeland,’ heritage, languages and ‘belonging’ are complex and dynamic, and they are constructed and reconstructed in different social and historical contexts; (2) the ways in which diasporic identities are constructed are shaped by the discourses that are available in the social context, and (3) the construction of diasporas and diasporic identities involves a complex interplay between the individual and the social context, in which the individual is an agent.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the situated construction and representation of diasporic trajectories in relation to the languages and ideologies of language that are part of the social and political landscape of Greece, and of the diaspora.
the ways that language resources are deployed in the construction of diasporas and diasporic identities.
the ways in which language and migration are intertwined, and how this is played out in the lives and experiences of migrants and their children, and in the communities in which they live.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this article has shown how a sociolinguistic approach to narratives about ‘homeland’ can provide insight into the complex ways in which language and identity intersect in diasporic contexts.

this research has provided a rich insight into the ways in which language and identity are intertwined, and the ways in which these are shaped and reshaped by the socio-political contexts of the diaspora, the ‘host’ country and the ‘homeland’.
the Pontian Greek diaspora in Northern Greece is a very interesting case study for sociolinguistic research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the study has shown how the participants’ narratives were constructed through the interplay between the different discourses of language, heritage and homeland, and their own agency.

the research participants were not just ‘passive victims’ of the diasporas they were in, but rather active participants in the creation of their own diasporic identities and in the construction of their own narratives.

the research findings have provided a more nuanced understanding of language and identity in the diaspora and in the ‘homeland’, which has implications for the development of language and identity studies, and for policy-making in the areas of language and migration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diasporic experience is complex and multifaceted, and that it is crucial to engage with the voices of those involved, and to listen to them.
, while there may be commonalities between different diasporas, it is important to recognise the specificity of the diasporic experience and the ways in which it is shaped by the social context.

the diaspora is a dynamic and complex space of social and linguistic interaction and that it can only be understood through an ethnographic approach that takes account of the situated and embodied nature of the social and linguistic practices of its members.
